name: VHDL

claims.claim_text: Very low gate-count programmable logic parts are configured through a graphical design entry tool in which lookup tables and flip-flops are dragged and dropped and wired up, rather than through VHDL or Verilog; at that gate count the effort of a hardware description language buys nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a nice little graphical interface where you drag and drop, you know, drag and drop a little lookup table and a flip-flop
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Silego, ADCs & Seismic Detection - Dave's Dingo Dystocia

claims.claim_text: A large offshore supply of VHDL coding labour exists, sustained by graduate volume, and it competes on hourly rate and turnaround. The countervailing cost is quality: cheap logic that has to be limped along and supported afterwards can outweigh the saving on the hours.
claims.quote_verbatim: places like India are churning out a hell of a lot of software specialists. You know, they, they, especially in the VHDL side of things. And, and I know they're sort of really taking over that market of doing that sort of coding and things like that
claims.episode_title: Idiorhythmic IPC Inconcinnity

claims.claim_text: VHDL supports a purely software-side career in hardware: some practitioners work only in the simulated domain, writing test benches and algorithms, and never take a design to physical hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: I know people in the VHDL domain who just live in the soft domain. They, all they're doing is writing test benches and, and doing algorithms and, you know, that wouldn't be me
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Aggravating Agersia Agiotage

claims.claim_text: Free vendor toolchains from Xilinx, Altera, Lattice and Actel are sufficient to learn VHDL, and they ship extensive tutorials with the software; for experience that carries commercial value the recommendation is to learn on one of the two large vendors' toolchains rather than a minor one.
claims.quote_verbatim: the free tools from Xilinx and Altera and probably Lattice and Actel probably have stuff too. But if you want to get some experience that's going to be valuable long-term, you'd have to pick one of Xilinx and Altera. They include extensive tutorials in their software
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Programmable logic distributors staff field application engineers with FPGA expertise who will write VHDL for a customer to get a design running, which is how companies without in-house FPGA skill obtain it.
claims.quote_verbatim: One of these FPGA distributors, they'll have an expert who can, you know, write you some VHDL for you to get you up and running
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Distribution, Wozniak & Robots - Early Eight-bit Endgame

claims.claim_text: A commercial FPGA module platform partitions the device: fixed vendor IP occupies the bus interface and DRAM, a window is left for high-level graphical code, and a second window is left for user VHDL that interfaces to the analogue circuit. The user's VHDL is the low-level layer that configures the clocking chip, monitors temperature and captures ADC data, and the vendor documents the timing and mechanical constraints for it in a module developer kit.
claims.quote_verbatim: the FPGA has fixed IP for the, the bus interface, the DRAM, the things that are always there. Uh, it has kind of a window where you can plug in your LabVIEW code and it has a window where you can plug in your, uh, low level logic that interfaces to your circuit
claims.speaker: Ryan Brown
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Brown - Effortless Equipment Extensibility

claims.claim_text: An engineer trained in Verilog can be moved onto a VHDL product and ship it within about three months, learning by doing; the VHDL content of successive digital test instrument cards was largely similar, covering streaming data to and from the host CPU, constructing test patterns, and checking for errors in responses.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had a product and a deadline that required VHDL. So I kind of switched at that point. Nice. Yep. And, you know, learning by doing. And in three months, we shipped it
claims.speaker: Ryan Brown
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan Brown - Effortless Equipment Extensibility

claims.claim_text: The two hardware description languages coexist inside a single project, with a designer using both at once; a VHDL test bench carries over to a different target's tool set only partially, so verification effort does not fully transfer when the design moves from FPGA to gate array.
claims.quote_verbatim: Are the test benches transferable? Like, can you use the VHDL test bench on the Gatorade tools? To some degree, yeah
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Multi-gigabit transceiver characterisation is done from inside the design: a vendor plugin instantiated in the user's VHDL taps the FPGA die's 10 Gbit transceiver and streams the raw recovered data to a PC application that computes average and peak bit error rate over days of running. Every parameter is tweakable, so the same setup can be tuned until almost any link passes, and results are only meaningful with the tweaks and the temperature stated.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's a plugin you get in your VHDL and you, and you can tap into the, um, uh, transceiver. Yeah. The actual, you know, the 10 gig bit transceiver on the FPGA die, and you can extract the raw data out of it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Contextual Electronics, ClubJameco and Solderpaste - Lifelong Learning Likelihood

claims.claim_text: VHDL describes hardware at the level of individual registers and logic structures, which is the source of the fine control that makes programmable logic worth using. The same level becomes a liability for arithmetic-heavy work such as DSP, where hand-coding every function at register level each time is avoided in favour of a generator that emits the VHDL.
claims.quote_verbatim: VHDL and Verilog, they can go down really low, and you actually, you know, create registers, and you can actually, you know, create structures in logic
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: A common DSP path into programmable logic never has the engineer writing the hardware description at all: the algorithm is built as a block model in Simulink, the model is converted to VHDL, and the VHDL is pushed into the FPGA. Simulink sits at a much higher abstraction level than C, so the effective design language is the block diagram.
claims.quote_verbatim: I did it from Simulink, doing Simulink down to, and then that converted to VHDL and then you push that down into a FPGA. Right. And then that actually, you know, did the signal processing
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Solar, FPGAs and Maxim Integrated - Solar Shopper Sickness

claims.claim_text: FPGA blocksets for Simulink, sold from around 2004 by Synplify and by Xilinx, let a designer assemble a math model graphically and emit VHDL or Verilog from it. The generated code makes the flow usable by an engineer who does not know the language well, but it is not maintainable source, so the model rather than the VHDL becomes the artefact that must be kept.
claims.quote_verbatim: you drop, like, these FPGA blocks into Simulink, and then you could basically create, like, these math models, and then, you know, tweak it, and then it would just basically spit out VHDL at Verilog, which is great for an idiot like me. Not great for making maintainable code
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: Legacy processor cores can be reimplemented from the ground up in VHDL and shipped in silicon without royalty exposure where the relevant patents have lapsed or the core was released: the 6502's instruction-set and mnemonic patents have long expired and Intel placed the 8051 in the public domain, whereas embedding an ARM core costs a per-unit royalty or a fixed fee negotiated up front for very large volumes.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can, you fire up your very long, your very long tool, your VHDL tool. And you're going to define from the ground up, something that implements the instruction set of a 6502
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: VHDL usage follows a geographic and sector split rather than a technical one: it predominates east of the Mississippi and across Europe, while Verilog predominates on the United States west coast and in Asia, and military work is largely VHDL.
claims.quote_verbatim: you got the obvious bifurcation that everything to the west and California and I think Asia is Verilog and everything to the east. You know, east of the Mississippi all the way over to Europe is VHDL. Yeah, all the military stuff is VHDL, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: Language choice among users of a development board is set by the language of the supplied example code rather than by the users' own evaluation: a vendor providing all of its examples in VHDL sees its customers converge on VHDL.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of my people eventually get over to VHDL because I provide all my examples that way
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: With the right macros and abstractions in place, an entire microcontroller can be described in a couple of hundred lines of VHDL that another engineer can read through and recognise as a processor, which matters because hardware description source is read far more often than it is written.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've seen entire microcontrollers described in, you know, a couple of hundred lines of VHDL because they've got the abstractions right, they've got the macros right that they put into their code, and you can read through it and say, yeah, I see how that is a processor
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

claims.claim_text: An open soft core distributed as VHDL source, such as the ZPUino, serves as an alternative to a vendor's own processor core, whose tooling is closed and not available to modify without a full licence. Because the source is open, custom peripherals slide into the core easily: a simple RGB LED controller added as a peripheral generates the PWM waveforms continuously in logic, so the processor only pokes it occasionally instead of driving the waveforms itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's all VHDL. It's all open. And you can slide your own peripherals into it pretty easily
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: Impedance Matching" with Davidson and Vandenbout - Presbytes Pushing Portfolios

claims.claim_text: The delta cycle is a VHDL feature governing the state analysis of how concurrent processes interact within a simulation time step; Verilog implements the same idea differently. Understanding it is the dividing line in a designer's competence, since the error rate in written code drops sharply once the model is internalised.
claims.quote_verbatim: the fundamental difference between Verilog and VHDL is something called the Delta cycle. Some of a feature that VHDL has, but Verilog implements it somewhat differently. And it's, it's the fundamental like state analysis of how your processes interact with each other
claims.speaker: Mark Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: When a VHDL design does not fit the target device, the two options are a larger FPGA or optimisation of the description itself; a logic analyser design that initially fitted only two channels was optimised rather than moved to a bigger part, over roughly four months of work before it fitted.
claims.quote_verbatim: about four months before it fit, about two channels would fit. Um, so the options were, uh, get a bigger FPGA or, or make it better
claims.speaker: Mark Garrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Joe and Mark Garrison - Subtly Spelling SayLeeAy

claims.claim_text: Becoming able to program in VHDL is a formal-learning task measured in weeks of concentrated effort, unlike the incremental daily accumulation of engineering knowledge from reading and browsing.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'm going to learn how to program in VHDL, right? And, yeah, right, you've got to go spend, you know, weeks and weeks at it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Is This A Show?

claims.claim_text: VHDL was built to support verification to a degree Verilog's syntax does not allow, extending to theoretical proofs that a piece of hardware will function as specified. The practical consequence is a mixed-language division of labour in which the design is written in Verilog and the test benches are written in VHDL.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can do a lot more verification. So like even theoretical proofs that, that this hardware will function as it should. And you can't do that because of the syntax of Verilog
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: VHDL requires substantially more syntax and boilerplate than Verilog for the same design. In textbooks that print equivalent implementations side by side, the Verilog page is around ninety per cent white space while the VHDL page fills entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's absolutely equivalent code. And then the Verilog is 90% white space. And then VHDL is, is fills up the page entirely to do the exact same
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: The two languages are close enough that an engineer fluent in Verilog can write working VHDL with reference material to hand; the cost of moving between them is syntactic rather than conceptual.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you know Verilog and you have, uh, Google handing to you, you'll be able to write VHDL. It's not, it's not that different. You can, you can, uh, go from one to the other
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: VHDL is more capable than Verilog in some respects, and the price of that capability is paid in declaration duplication: the same information must be restated in several places in the source, which is the specific reason engineers who prefer C-like syntax choose Verilog instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: VHDL is, I don't like the verboseness of it. But there are certain advantages in some. It's more capable in some ways, but I'm just, I like nice syntax and not duplicating a lot of things like you do in VHDL
claims.speaker: David Kronstein
claims.episode_title: An Interview with David Kronstein (Tesla500)

claims.claim_text: VHDL will not accept a name that has not been declared and matched everywhere it appears, so a mistyped signal identifier stops the tool rather than silently producing an additional object. The strictness is what makes VHDL slow to write and is also what removes an entire class of defect before simulation.
claims.quote_verbatim: I came from the VHDL world where it's like, you can't type a single thing unless it's like, you know, if they like type it in multiple places and it checks everything and everything has to be like perfect
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Pulled From A Working Environment

claims.claim_text: VHDL is strongly typed and explicit: a signal must effectively be stated in three places with all of them matching, and the tool reports at length when they do not. That redundancy is the direct cause of the language's verbosity.
claims.quote_verbatim: VHDL is very complainy. I know that from my past. Yeah. So I'm pretty sure when I say this, that VHDL is strongly type. Someone will probably correct me, but it is way more verbose
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Craig J Bishop

claims.claim_text: Open-source FPGA toolchains support Verilog more thoroughly than VHDL, and the stock of existing example code and reusable cores is larger in Verilog, so choosing VHDL narrows the available tools and reference designs; VHDL cores do exist but in smaller number. Engineers who began in VHDL commonly switch when they start working with United States companies or on open-source projects.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the open source tools, um, use Verilog more than VHDL. So you, you will have more choices
claims.speaker: Sylvain Minot
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: Migen is a Python toolbox for building complex digital hardware that functions as a Python-to-VHDL compiler, generating the hardware description from a higher-level program rather than replacing the downstream flow.
claims.quote_verbatim: a generator tool for FPGA stuff, right? So it's kind of like a higher level, yeah, Python toolbox for building complex digital hardware
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Setting Fire To The Tracks

claims.claim_text: VHDL was the default language for FPGA work through roughly the mid-2000s, and the balance has since moved: chip industry work is now predominantly Verilog, with VHDL retaining a substantial minority of it rather than disappearing.
claims.quote_verbatim: the chip industry is using Verilog mostly. I think that it's, you know, it's a little. So it won the war, you think? Uh, it's never going to be like all, all or nothing
claims.episode_title: Pulled From A Working Environment

claims.claim_text: In the first Tiny Tapeout run, roughly thirty to forty per cent of submitted designs were written in a hardware description language, and the submission flow had to be split into separate automated build paths for Verilog, Amaranth and VHDL, since a shared entry point could not cover all three.
claims.quote_verbatim: we actually ended up with maybe 30 or 40% of the designs were in some HDL or other. And we ended up changing the, the GitHub action so that there was like one version for Verilog and one version for Amaranth and one version for VHDL or whatever
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: The VHDL and Verilog abstraction has held as a universal standard across decades of process and vendor change: RTL written without vendor-specific IP blocks can be pushed through different vendors' FPGA flows and, with care, through an ASIC flow without modification. The abstraction is harder to work in than a general-purpose programming language such as Python, and that difficulty is separate from its durability.
claims.quote_verbatim: If I wrote the right RTL code and I can run that on a, you know, different vendors, FPGA devices, even if I'm careful, take the same Verilog code and, and use an ASIC without, you know, without changing anything
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson
